name: Temporal
summary: An open-source durable execution engine: you write workflows as ordinary code and they survive crashes.
intro: In Temporal you write a workflow as normal code in Go, Java, TypeScript, Python, .NET, PHP, Ruby or Rust. Anything with side effects, such as charging a card or sending an email, goes in an activity. Your own worker processes poll task queues on the Temporal Service, run the code, and report each step back, and the service records every step in the workflow’s event history. If a worker dies, another one replays that history to rebuild the workflow’s state and carries on from the same line. A 30-day sleep or a wait for a signal uses no worker while it waits.

Because of replay, workflow code must be deterministic: no direct network calls, clock reads or random numbers outside the SDK’s own APIs. Activities get timeouts and automatic retries with backoff. The server is open source under the MIT licence, written in Go, and stores its state in PostgreSQL, MySQL or Cassandra. Temporal Cloud runs the service for you, priced by actions, while your workers and data stay in your own infrastructure.
strengths: Workflows are real code: loops, branches, error handling and unit tests in your own language
Built for long-running processes: durable timers, signals and queries let a workflow wait days for a person or another system
Self-host it or use Temporal Cloud with the same SDKs, and run your workers on Kubernetes, VMs, serverless platforms or your own hardware
You can replay a production event history locally to debug exactly what happened
limits: The determinism rule takes discipline, and changing code while old executions are still running needs explicit versioning
One execution’s history is capped at 51,200 events or 50 MB; long loops must restart themselves with Continue-As-New
Self-hosting means running a distributed service plus its database, and tuning both
You run and scale the workers yourself, even on Temporal Cloud

story: Temporal’s founders worked on the same problem for two decades. Maxim Fateev joined Amazon in 2002, when the entire website was one binary, and his team built the publish/subscribe infrastructure that grew into SQS. Queues alone didn’t make communication between services reliable, so he went on to lead the Simple Workflow Service (SWF), and Samar Abbas joined the team that brought SWF to the public in 2012. SWF was conceptually advanced, but “developers found it complex and cumbersome.” Abbas then built the open-source Durable Task Framework at Microsoft, which became a key dependency of Azure Functions.

In 2015 the two reunited at Uber and built Cadence, a workflow engine in which workflows are ordinary code. It grew to more than 100 internal use cases in three years before going open source in 2017. In 2019 they left Uber to build Temporal, which started as a fork of Cadence, and Temporal 1.0 shipped on September 29, 2020.

Temporal named its idea Durable Execution: the platform keeps a workflow’s full state, so the code carries on after any failure. Interest jumped with AI agents, which run long multi-step tasks, and in September 2026 the company raised $550 million at a $12.55 billion valuation.

choices.choice: Workflows as ordinary code, not a DSL
choices.why: SWF taught its creators that power without a good developer experience doesn’t get adopted. In Go, Java or Python you keep loops, tests and your usual tools; Fateev says you end up “writing pure business logic”.

choices.choice: An event history replayed by workers
choices.why: The service records every step, and a fresh worker rebuilds a workflow’s state by re-running the code against that history. That gives crash recovery and exact debugging, and it’s why workflow code must be deterministic.
The service stores state and hands out tasks, while your code and data stay on your own machines, so the same workflow runs against a self-hosted server or Temporal Cloud.
Fateev had watched powerful technologies stagnate at Amazon when they were kept proprietary, so Cadence was fully open source and Temporal kept it under the MIT licence.
